Photograph: Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images Grenada Family of British man found dead in Grenada ask local police to work with UK investigators Andrew Frederick’s body was found in property he was staying at in Grenada in January Natricia Duncan and agencies Wed 9 Sep 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 04.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death. Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at in Grenada on 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide. In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”. After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out. The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”. At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death. The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”. In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick. “We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said. Family accuse UK government of lack of support over death of Briton in Grenada Read more It added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson. He leaves behind his cherished daughter, who should be growing up with him beside her, not learning to live without him. “Our family remain determined to uncover the truth about what happened to Andrew and to see justice follow. We hope this ruling is the step that finally enables a complete, properly coordinated investigation and that everyone who can assist will now do so.” Earlier this year, the family had called for an urgent review of the policies governing UK assistance to the loved ones of Britons killed abroad, after they were forced to launch their own public appeals for information, and commission an independent forensic pathologist and a private investigation. “Eight months have passed since Andrew was taken from us. In that time, we have learned what no family should ever have to learn, and fought battles no family should ever face alone,” their statement said. It added: “We have relentlessly sought answers and support while carrying the weight of Andrew’s loss and the horror of what was done to him. We still do not have a complete account of what happened, and important questions remain unanswered. “We hope the Grenadian authorities with knowledge of the case will now share that information and work collaboratively with the Metropolitan police, allowing the investigation to proceed without further delay. We are also seeking urgent answers as to why Andrew’s organs were absent when his body was returned to the UK for further examination.” In Grenada, the Office of the Commissioner told the Guardian that “the matter will be progressing to the coroner’s court for the parish of Saint George”. A Met spokesperson said: “The Met is investigating the death of 47-year-old Andrew Donald Frederick, who died in Grenada on 4 January. “Mr Frederick’s family are being supported by specialist officers. “No arrests have been made at this stage and inquiries are ongoing.” Officers have contacted the Royal Grenada Police Force (RGPF) to offer assistance and discuss how the investigation can be progressed. Inquest proceedings have been suspended pending the outcome of police investigations. https://bnn-news.com/bnn-in-focus/bnn-in.text: Photo: MI caricature Advertisements Reinis Uzulnieks’ journey from a pre-election debate in Īslīce parish and a visit to the ZZS campaign tent in Bauska to Stopiņi parish, where police stopped him behind the wheel while heavily intoxicated, highlights a much bigger problem than one former minister’s excessive drinking. Behind the scenes, stories have repeatedly circulated about the drinking habits of one powerful figure or another. Yet in most cases there have been no consequences, even when everyone knows that the boss failed to turn up for work because he was drunk. Does Latvia have any chance of ridding itself of this drinking problem among high-ranking officials? BNN put the question to Filips Rajevskis, political scientist and co-founder of the company Mediju tilts. “Overall, our society consumes a great deal of alcohol,” Rajevskis says, pointing as an example to the work by Dr. hist. Gatis Krūmiņš, a leading researcher at Vidzeme University of Applied Sciences, titled Who is stronger, Latvians or alcohol? A brief look at the events of the past 200 years, which examines alcohol consumption in detail. “We can see it clearly in the statistics as well. Even one of our folk songs says: ‘I drank with my own money, I rode my own horse.’ So historically, we have liked to drink. The problem is that alcohol consumption increased dramatically during the Soviet era – the population was encouraged to drink, and that was part of the policy. The drinking culture and, most importantly, the amount of alcohol consumed increased by roughly two and a half to three times compared with pre-war Latvia.” “We inherited a society that drinks, and that does not disappear within a single generation. Drinking becomes part of the culture. Many people drink, and some drink heavily. If the ‘green dragon’ of alcohol is present in every sphere of society, why would it not be present in politics as well? Advertisements Politicians are members of the same society, and the political environment is a mirror of society,” Rajevskis explains. Asked how this problem could be eradicated from society and, even more importantly, from political life, the political scientist says the issue is extremely complicated and cannot be solved through restrictions alone. “Of course, the simplest solution may seem to be raising prices through excise duties, introducing more restrictions and reducing the availability of alcohol. But we can clearly see what has happened with tobacco products – prices have been increased significantly, many things have been banned, and the result is a huge black market.” “The same would happen with alcohol. If prices are raised significantly, people will drink illegal homemade alcohol. No one has managed to eliminate the problem that way. What we are talking about here is a much broader fight against alcoholism as an addiction. It is a problem for society as a whole. Of course, when it comes to public officials, penalties should be particularly severe precisely because public officials represent the state.” Advertisements Rajevskis also draws attention to another problem – the tolerance within society and political circles towards people who drink excessively. “The Uzulnieks story itself has already been discussed from every possible angle. He drove drunk, he was caught, there will be criminal consequences, he will lose his driving licence and there will also be consequences involving the car. What happens next in that respect is fairly clear.” “But then there is the question of the people who were with him that day, who tolerated it and did nothing when he got behind the wheel. People can tell all sorts of stories, but three and a half per mille does not suddenly appear after one glass of wine, one beer or one glass of spirits. More than three per mille means that a person has already been heavily intoxicated for some time.” “And then the question becomes one of everyone else’s tolerance. Nobody says: listen, mate, don’t get behind the wheel, you’re going to get into trouble, I’ll drive you. It simply demonstrates society’s broader attitude: well, go ahead, what does it have to do with me? We are fortunate that all of this ended only with a ruined career, a huge penalty and the loss of a driving licence, rather than a horrific road accident and lives being destroyed,” Rajevskis says. Advertisements After Uzulnieks was detained, people suddenly began coming forward saying that his friendship with the “green dragon” had been known for a long time. If that was the case, the question arises: why was a minister with such a drinking problem not taken out of the picture earlier? Did everyone know and simply turn a blind eye to avoid airing their dirty laundry in public? Rajevskis again stresses that the former minister was hardly living the life of a monk, quietly drinking somewhere out of sight. “He had a very active social life. And that raises the question of all these people’s tolerance when, for example, he had been drinking heavily. It demonstrates the tolerance of society as a whole. There is not enough public demand for the attitude that this is unacceptable, that public officials simply cannot behave this way.” Advertisements BNN asked whether parliamentary candidates should at least be required to provide confirmation or a medical certificate from an addiction specialist showing that they do not have an alcohol or drug addiction. Rajevskis replied that this would neither address the essence of the problem nor provide a solution. “Then we might as well start talking about ministers having to begin every working day by blowing into a breathalyser or something like that,” the political scientist says ironically. “Everything starts with reducing society’s tolerance of people functioning while intoxicated. There is essentially no other instrument – society’s overall attitude has to change.” One question remains: Reinis Uzulnieks is still standing in the election and could potentially be elected to parliament. The former welfare minister was relatively popular, and it cannot be ruled out that he could perform well in the election despite the drinking scandal and his departure from ZZS. Advertisements “I would not be surprised if he were elected. But there is one problem – a criminal conviction could mean the loss of his mandate, and his case has already been referred for criminal prosecution,” Rajevskis says. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmq8.text: Image source, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images By Grace Eliza Goodwin Published 15 October 2026, 20:13 BST Updated 2 minutes ago Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US. The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received. Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters. Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail. "This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday. Delaware's Department of Elections said its office received and opened a letter containing a white powdery substance on Thursday, adding that staff followed security protocols on handling suspicious mail. The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder. The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it. Senator Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was also sent a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted before reaching the office, his spokesman said. The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC. The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress. Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages . A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states.
